1107.title: Halakha, the path you walk
1107.hook: halakha, Jewish law, heard as a path: decided by majority and precedent
1107.carry: halakha is a path, walked step by step
1107.howItsDone: Jews who keep halakha look to it for how to live day to day, from food and prayer to business and family life, and often bring their questions to a rabbi, who weighs the majority view and earlier rulings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: the minority is kept. The losing view stays on the page, labeled. Today a new stretch begins: how Jewish law actually gets decided.

Across a park there's a path nobody paved. No sign put it there. It's just where people walk, worn into the grass by one pair of shoes after another, until it's the obvious way across. Newcomers follow it without thinking. It's not the only way through the park, but it's the way people take, and the more feet on it, the clearer it gets. Yesterday the Mishnah kept the minority's words. But on an ordinary morning, a person has to know what to actually do. Today's word carries a path inside it.
screen: `A PATH WORN INTO GRASS.` → `THE WAY PEOPLE TAKE.` → `BUT WHAT DO I DO TODAY?`

segments.voice: Halakha. It's the Hebrew name for Jewish law, the practical answer to how to live. First, what readers hear in it. Tradition hears in the word the Hebrew verb for walking. In Exodus, Moses's father-in-law, Jethro, advises him to show the people, in the King James wording, "the way wherein they must walk." So the law is pictured not as a wall of rules but as a path, walked step by step, every day. Second, how a path gets chosen. The sages read a verse in Exodus about not following a crowd to do wrong, and drew from it a working rule: in a dispute among judges, go with the majority. Third, the majority isn't the whole story. You met this verdict long ago, in tractate Eruvin: the schools of Hillel and Shammai argue for a long time, and a voice from heaven declares, these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the school of Hillel. Both are words of the living God, but you can only walk one path at a time. And why Hillel? The Talmud says they were gentle and humble, and taught the words of the school of Shammai too, even putting Shammai's words before their own. Fourth, precedent. Once a path is walked, later teachers look at how earlier ones ruled and walk where they walked, the way a newcomer follows the worn path in the grass. Halakha isn't only a list. It's a road with a lot of footprints already on it.
screen: `A PATH, NOT A WALL.` · `GO WITH THE MAJORITY.` · `THESE AND THESE; THE LAW FOLLOWS HILLEL.` · `FOOTPRINTS ALREADY ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `HALAKHA IS A PATH.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and take a few slow steps across the room and back, feeling each foot land; if you'd rather stay seated, press your feet into the floor, one and then the other. Either way, choose a direction before you move, and notice that choosing one doesn't make the others disappear. You're just going this way, now.
Halakha. Jewish law, heard as a path to walk, decided by the majority and carried forward by precedent. Today's word.
Your line: halakha is a path, walked step by step. Chosen with the majority, followed in the footprints. One more step up the hill.

1108.title: Custom
1108.hook: a community's custom can carry the weight of law
1108.howItsDone: Jewish communities keep their own customs in prayer, food and holidays, and families pass down their minhagim. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities, for example, follow different customs on a number of practices, and communities often treat their own as binding for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, halakha, and your line: the way you walk. The law as a path, chosen by the majority, worn in by precedent. Today, the paths a single town or family wears in for itself.

It's the morning before Passover in two neighboring towns. In one, the shops are open and the workshops busy until noon, the way they always are. In the next town over, people have put their tools down. Same holiday, same Torah, different mornings. Now a carpenter from the first town walks into the second, ready to work. Is he doing something wrong? Is the second town too strict? The Mishnah takes up this very case, and its answer doesn't come from a verse. It comes from what each town does.
screen: `THE MORNING BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `ONE TOWN WORKS, ONE RESTS.` → `A CARPENTER CROSSES OVER.`

segments.voice: Minhag. It's the Hebrew word for custom, the practice a community has taken on, and in Jewish law it can carry real weight. First, the Mishnah, in tractate Pesachim. Where people are accustomed to work on the eve of Passover until midday, they work. Where they're accustomed not to, they don't. The place decides. Second, the traveler. Someone who goes from one kind of place to the other, the Mishnah says, takes on the stricter practice of both the place he left and the place he's in. And it adds a reason that's not about rules at all: a person shouldn't stand out against local custom, because of the quarrels it can cause. Custom keeps the peace of a community. Third, custom can outlast its reason. The Talmud, in tractate Beitzah, tells of Jews outside the land of Israel who kept an extra festival day, because long ago they couldn't be sure of the calendar in time. Later the calendar was known. Should they drop the extra day? The answer sent to them: be careful with the custom of your ancestors that is in your hands. Fourth, a family is a community too. One family keeps a dish for one holiday, another lights candles a certain way, a third sings a tune nobody else knows. The law leaves room for these, and communities hold them as their own. A path walked by your grandparents isn't nothing.

1109.title: A fence around the Torah
1109.hook: rabbis add protective rules around Torah laws
1109.howItsDone: Rabbinic rules often work as fences: for example, the sages added Sabbath rules that keep people well back from the work the Torah forbids, and Jews who keep them treat the fences as part of the law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, minhag, and your line: custom is law too. Today, rules built on purpose, not by habit: fences.

At the top of a cliff there's a beautiful view, and a sheer drop. Nobody puts the warning at the very edge; by the time you're reading it there, one bad step is all it takes. So the railing goes in a few feet back. You can still see everything. You just can't stumble over. It isn't the cliff. It's what keeps you from the cliff. The opening teaching of Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, asks the sages to build one of these.
screen: `A VIEW, AND A DROP.` → `THE RAILING GOES IN FEET BACK.` → `NOT THE CLIFF, THE RAILING.`

segments.voice: Seyag. It's the Hebrew word for a fence, and in Jewish law it names a protective rule the sages add around a Torah law to keep people from breaking it. First, the source, which you met long ago: the first mishnah of Avot tells the sages to be careful in judgment, to raise up many students, and to make a fence around the Torah. Second, what one looks like. On the Sabbath, as the sages read the Torah, a person may not carry things out from a house into the street. The Mishnah in tractate Shabbat adds a rule for Friday: a tailor shouldn't go out with his needle close to dark, in case he forgets it's there and carries it once the Sabbath begins. The fence sits a little way back from the edge. Third, fences can go too far, and the tradition says so itself. In the garden, God told Adam not to eat from the tree. But when Eve repeats the command, she adds something: "neither shall ye touch it." A teaching in Avot de-Rabbi Natan imagines Adam built that fence, and the serpent used it. It pushed her against the tree: you touched it and nothing happened, so eating won't hurt either. The lesson the sages draw: don't make the fence more important than what it guards, or when the fence falls, the garden goes with it. Fourth, fences aren't only legal. Rabbi Akiva, also in Avot, names others: tradition is a fence for the Torah, and silence is a fence for wisdom.
screen: `MAKE A FENCE AROUND THE TORAH.` · `THE TAILOR'S NEEDLE BEFORE DARK.` · `NEITHER SHALL YE TOUCH IT.` · `SILENCE, A FENCE FOR WISDOM.` · then, large: `A FENCE AROUND THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you want to protect, like sleep, a morning walk or an hour without a screen, and find the cliff edge, the moment it usually slips away. Then step back from it: what small rule, set earlier, would keep you from the edge, like the phone out of the bedroom? Keep it small, and remember which is the fence and which is the garden.
Seyag. A fence: a protective rule the sages set around a Torah law, so people stay far from breaking it. Today's word.
Your line: a fence around the law. A fence is a kindness to your future self. See you tomorrow.

1110.title: Biblical and rabbinic
1110.hook: laws from the Torah and laws from the rabbis carry different weight
1110.howItsDone: When a rabbi answers a question of Jewish law, the source of the rule matters: a doubt about a Torah law is usually resolved strictly, and a doubt about a rabbinic law may be resolved leniently. The Hanukkah blessing is said over a rabbinic command.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seyag, and your line: a fence around the law. Fences are rules the sages built. Today, how the law tells a fence from what it guards.

On each night of Hanukkah, before the candles are lit, a blessing is said. It thanks God, who made us holy with commandments and commanded us to light the Hanukkah light. Commanded us. Here's the puzzle: open the Torah from beginning to end and you won't find Hanukkah in it. The story belongs to a much later time. So where exactly did God command it? The Talmud asks that very question, out loud, in tractate Shabbat. The answer opens up a distinction Jewish law leans on, day after day.
screen: `WHO COMMANDED US TO LIGHT.` → `NO HANUKKAH IN THE TORAH.` → `SO WHERE WAS IT COMMANDED?`

segments.voice: D'oraita. It's an Aramaic word meaning from the Torah, and it names a law that comes from the Torah itself. Its partner is d'rabbanan, from the rabbis: a law the sages set. First, the difference in source. Keeping the Sabbath, eating matzah on the first night of Passover: the Talmud treats these as d'oraita, from the verses. Lighting Hanukkah candles, and many of the fences you met yesterday: d'rabbanan. Second, the puzzle. If Hanukkah is rabbinic, how can the blessing say God commanded us? The Talmud gives two answers, from two sages. One points to Deuteronomy, where the people are told not to turn aside from what the judges of their day teach them. The other points to a verse in the Song of Moses: ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say. Either way, the rabbis' rulings carry authority because the Torah itself sends people to their teachers. Rabbinic law isn't a stranger; it's a command to listen. Third, the weights really are different, and you see it when things are unclear. The Talmud's working rule: in doubt about a Torah law, lean strict. In doubt about a rabbinic law, you may lean lenient. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Knowing the source tells you how to act when life gets messy: when you're unsure, when there's illness, when two duties collide. A rule's weight depends on where it came from.

1111.title: Early codes
1111.hook: the Rif and the Rosh summarize the Talmud's rulings
1111.howItsDone: Students of Jewish law study the Rif and the Rosh alongside the Talmud to see how its discussions were turned into rulings, and later codes of law cite them often.

segments.voice: Yesterday, d'oraita, and your line: different weights. From the Torah, or from the rabbis, and in doubt the weights differ. Today, a problem: how do you find the ruling at all?

A woman in a small town has a practical question, something about her kitchen before a holiday. She knows the answer is in the Talmud somewhere. But the Talmud, as you've seen, is a conversation: a question, a challenge, a story, a side road, a question left standing. The answer might be on this page, or argued across several tractates. Her rabbi can find it. But what about a town with no great scholar, or a student just starting out? Somebody has to walk through the conversation and write down where it lands.
screen: `A PRACTICAL QUESTION.` → `THE ANSWER IS IN THE CONVERSATION.` → `WHERE DOES IT LAND?`

segments.voice: Early codes. It's the name this path gives to early summaries of the Talmud's rulings, and two of them are known by short names: the Rif and the Rosh. First, the names. Jewish tradition often calls its teachers by their initials. The Rif is Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, whose name ties him to the city of Fez. The Rosh is Rabbenu Asher, son of Yehiel. Second, what the Rif did. He walked through the Talmud tractate by tractate, in its own order, and kept the Talmud's own words, but only the ones that lead to a ruling. The long back-and-forth, the side roads, much of the story: trimmed away. What's left reads like the Talmud with the scaffolding taken down. Third, what the Rosh did. He followed the Rif's path but brought in the voices that came after, including the Tosafot you met a few days ago, and weighed them, so his summary carries more of the conversation into the ruling. Fourth, where you find them: often at the back of a printed Talmud volume, after the tractate. The full conversation in front, the summary behind. And a summary is a set of choices. Every line the Rif kept, he kept on purpose, and every line he dropped, he judged not needed for practice. Later scholars argued with those choices, which is its own kind of conversation. A good summary doesn't replace the long version. It's a path through it.

1112.title: Maimonides' code
1112.hook: the Mishneh Torah sets out Jewish law in one voice, without citing sources
1112.howItsDone: Students learn the Mishneh Torah alone or in classes, and some follow a daily study cycle through it. Printed editions surround the text with commentaries that trace each ruling back to its sources.

segments.voice: Yesterday, early codes: the Rif and the Rosh drew rulings out of the Talmud's long arguments. Your line was summaries. Today, a book that went much further.

No footnotes. For some readers that was the problem with this book, and for its author it was the point. Moses ben Maimon, called Maimonides in English and Rambam in Hebrew, set out to write down Jewish law in one orderly work, not only the laws people kept in his day, but the laws of the Temple and of kings too. And he wrote it as plain statements. This is required. This is forbidden. This is how it is done. No rabbi says, no trail back to the page it came from. After weeks of a Talmud full of voices, here is a book with one.
screen: `NO FOOTNOTES.` → `ALL OF THE LAW, IN ORDER.` → `ONE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Its name is Mishneh Torah, often rendered a repetition of the Torah. Turn it four ways. First, the voice. Where the Talmud keeps every side of an argument, Maimonides gives the ruling and moves on. In his introduction he explains why: a person could read the written Torah first, then this book, and know the oral law without needing another book in between. Second, where it begins: not with blessings or with Shabbat, but with God. The opening law, in the section on the foundations of the Torah, is to know that there is a First Being who brought all things into existence. Study, character and repentance sit in the same work as the laws of damages and of the Sabbath. For Maimonides, belief and behavior belong in one book. Third, who it was for. He wrote in clear, orderly Hebrew rather than the Talmud's Aramaic, and arranged everything by topic, so a learner could find a law without knowing where in the Talmud it lived. Fourth, the pushback. Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp critical notes on the code. Some worried that with no sources, nobody could check a ruling or follow its reasoning, and that people might stop learning the Talmud itself. And the twist: open a printed Mishneh Torah today and the Rabad's notes are there on the page, along with later commentaries that went back and traced each ruling to its source. The book without footnotes ended up surrounded by them.

1113.hook: Jacob ben Asher arranges law in four "rows", the model for later codes

1113.howItsDone: The Tur is studied in yeshivas and by students of Jewish law, often alongside the Beit Yosef, a commentary printed with it. Its four section names are still used to organize Jewish law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maimonides' code, and your line: a code for everyone. This week walked the road of Jewish law: halakha, custom, the fence, the weight of a rule, the early codes, and one book in one voice. Today, a different way to lay it out.

Gold settings, and in them, stones. The book of Exodus describes a breastplate for the high priest, a square of woven cloth set with precious stones in four rows, each stone engraved with the name of a tribe. The Torah lingers over it, stone by stone. Much later, a rabbi named Jacob ben Asher, a son of the Rosh you met two days ago, borrowed that picture for a book of law. He called it the Four Rows, and people came to call it by one short word.
screen: `A BREASTPLATE OF STONES.` → `FOUR ROWS.` → `A BOOK OF LAW BORROWS THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Tur. A row. The full name is Arba'ah Turim, the Four Rows, and each row takes its name from a phrase in scripture. The first row is Orach Chayim, the path of life: waking up, blessings, prayer, Shabbat, the festivals. The second is Yoreh De'ah, he will teach knowledge: questions people often bring to a rabbi, what may be eaten, how to mourn, how to give charity, how to study Torah. The third is Even HaEzer, the stone of help, named for the stone the prophet Samuel set up: marriage, divorce and family. The fourth is Choshen Mishpat, the breastplate of judgment: money, property, damages, the courts. There the image comes full circle: the last row is named for the breastplate the whole book is built on. Now notice what's missing. Maimonides set out the laws of the Temple and of kings. Jacob ben Asher left those aside and arranged the law that people could live by where they were. Notice, too, how he writes. Where Maimonides' code speaks in one voice, the Tur often names earlier authorities and lays their views side by side, and often gives his father's view. It's a code that still lets you hear a little of the conversation. And the shape lasted: tomorrow's book keeps the very same four rows. Prayer, food, family, money, and a whole life fits inside them.
